question: Why is the sky blue, but the sunset red?

scene.title: Why is the sky blue, but the sunset red?
scene.subtitle: Sunlight looks white, yet the sky glows blue and sunsets glow red. Both colours come from the way air sends light off in new directions.
scene.why: The blue sky shows something you cannot see directly: light is a wave, and the shorter the wave, the more the air sends it off course.
scene.opening: Sunlight looks white, yet the sky glows blue and sunsets glow red. Where do those colours come from?

beats.title: No air, no blue
beats.body: On the Moon, with no air, the daytime sky is black. On Earth the same sunlight crosses air, and the sky glows blue.

beats.title: Shaking electrons
beats.body: Light is a wave that shakes the electrons in each air molecule, and they scatter it in every direction. Blue’s shorter wave shakes them about as far as red, but more often, and scatters about six times as much.

beats.title: Blue from everywhere
beats.body: So all along its way, sunlight loses some of its blue to the air. That blue reaches your eyes from all over the sky.

beats.title: Red sunsets
beats.body: At sunset the light crosses about 38 times as much air to reach you. Almost all its blue is sent away on the way, but a quarter of the red is left, so the Sun looks red.

scene.takeaway: Air sends blue sunlight off in every direction far more than red, so blue comes at you from the whole sky. At sunset the light has crossed so much air that its blue is gone, leaving red and orange.

questions.q: Violet is scattered even more than blue. Why isn’t the sky violet?
questions.a: Sunlight has less violet than blue, and our eyes are less sensitive to it. The mix of scattered colours that reaches us looks sky blue.

questions.q: Why are clouds white, not blue?
questions.a: Unlike air molecules, cloud droplets are far bigger than light’s waves, so they scatter every colour about equally, and an equal mix looks white.

questions.q: Is air blue, like tinted glass?
questions.a: No. Blue glass turns the light passing through it blue by soaking up the red. Air does the opposite: light that crosses a lot of air turns orange, as at sunset. The blue sky is light sent sideways.
